title: Ganga holds out her son
hookLine: Shantanu finds a dam of arrows on the Ganga, and the river goddess brings him his son: why Hindus call the Ganga mother
carry: ganga is a mother, not just a river

cards: The Ganga has gone shallow. Shantanu notices it while he's out hunting, following a wounded deer along the bank. The great river is barely moving, as if something were holding it back.
Ganga left him long ago, carrying their baby into the water, and he has ruled alone since then. Now he forgets the deer and goes looking for the reason: what on earth could stop a river?

teach.b: By the water he finds a young man, tall and handsome, who has stopped the Ganga's flow with arrows, a dam of them across the current. Shantanu has no idea who this is.

The young man clouds the king's senses with a power of illusion, and vanishes. So Shantanu calls on Ganga: show me the child. And she rises from the river in a beautiful form, holding the young man by the hand.

This, she tells him, is your eighth son, the one I took with me. The text knows him by two names: Devavrata, and Gangeya, Ganga's son. Stay with that picture, because it's how Hindus have seen this river for centuries.
She's a goddess, and a mother: she rises out of her own current and hands a king his child. Hindus still call her Ganga Ma, Mother Ganga.
Pilgrims bathe in her at Haridwar and Varanasi, and every evening priests wave great lamps over her in the Ganga aarti.

Many families keep a little sealed pot or bottle of Ganga jal, Ganga water, at home: for pujas, for blessing a new house, for a few drops on the lips of someone who is dying. And many carry a loved one's ashes to her.

teach.h: GANGA IS A MOTHER, NOT JUST A RIVER.
teach.b: The teaching under it: in Hinduism the sacred can flow through the world itself, a river you can stand in, and you meet her the way you'd meet a mother, with reverence and love. This son will carry her name all his life.
For now, a king who lost eight sons is standing beside one of them, handed back by the river.

how: Many Hindu homes keep a small sealed pot or bottle of Ganga jal, water from the Ganga, for pujas, blessings and last rites, and evening Ganga aarti is offered on her banks at Haridwar and Varanasi.

games.q: you're Shantanu. a young stranger has dammed the river with arrows, then vanished. you wonder if he's your son. what do you do?
o: call on Ganga to show you the child.
send soldiers to search the banks.
games.why: he calls on Ganga, and the river herself rises like a mother, holding the young man by the hand: your eighth son.

practice: If you keep Ganga jal or any water for puja, pour a little into a cup; if not, ordinary water is fine. Hold it, and breathe in, remembering the river who rose to hand a father his son.
Breathe out and sprinkle a drop on your head, the way many Hindus do, with a quiet word of thanks to Ganga Ma. If you don't pray, simply hold the water and thank whatever has carried you this far.

wordCard.voice: Devavrata. Ganga's son, also called Gangeya, who held the river back with a dam of arrows before his father even knew his name.

orig.note: Sanskrit Devavrata, a name of Shantanu and Ganga's eighth son; the text also calls him Gangeya.

carryVoice: Your line: Ganga is a mother, not just a river. Tomorrow, who taught the boy while he was away. Day seven hundred eight, done.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (Shantanu finds the Ganga shallow; the youth and the arrows; Ganga presents their son)
Ganga honored as goddess and mother (Ganga Ma); Ganga jal kept at home; Ganga aarti at Haridwar and Varanasi; ashes immersed in the Ganga: standard Hindu practice
